target: AG1’s claim that AI will make work faster and more effective and thereby benefit workers and society economically
objection: AG2 argues that faster AI-assisted work often means fewer jobs, lower wages, automation of tasks, and greater concentration of profits in a few firms, which harms workers and small businesses rather than broadly helping the economy.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can serve as a practical accessibility tool without major downsides
objection: AG2 objects that accessibility AI often requires privacy tradeoffs, such as microphones, text and browsing collection, and behavioral or emotion inference, exposing vulnerable users to surveillance or misuse.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves health and workplace safety
objection: AG2 contends that these benefits are not guaranteed because AI systems can be biased and error-prone, and in high-stakes settings they can misdiagnose or misjudge risk, especially harming marginalized people.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps students and professionals work better
objection: AG2 argues that AI undermines critical thinking by encouraging people to rely on outputs for writing, studying, and decision-making, which reduces real reasoning practice and weakens educational outcomes.

target: AG1’s assumption that responsible design and use can easily contain AI harms
objection: AG2 says this is too weak a safeguard because market incentives usually favor rapid deployment and monetization, not careful prevention of privacy violations, bias, and labor displacement.

target: AG2’s claim that AI will inevitably cause job loss, lower wages, and labor harm
objection: AG1 replies that those harms are not inevitable because AI often augments work rather than replacing it, and societies can manage transitions through reskilling, job programs, and new AI-related roles.

target: AG2’s claim that AI-accessibility tools necessarily require harmful privacy tradeoffs
objection: AG1 objects that privacy risks are solvable through design and policy, such as on-device processing, meaningful consent, data minimization, transparency, and audits, so privacy concerns do not negate the value of accessibility tools.

target: AG2’s claim that AI will inevitably worsen health and safety outcomes
objection: AG1 argues that bias and error are reasons for stronger evaluation and human-in-the-loop safeguards, not reasons to reject AI, and that AI can improve triage and hazard detection when properly governed.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking in an unavoidable way
objection: AG1 counters that AI can be used as a tutor and feedback tool that explains concepts, generates practice problems, and checks understanding, so the issue is how AI is used, not whether it exists.

target: AG2’s claim that incentives make privacy, bias, and labor harms inevitable
objection: AG1 says this is an argument for regulation and governance, not for opposing AI outright, because auditing, privacy standards, accountability, and high-risk rules can be imposed.

target: AG1’s claim that risks can be adequately handled by governance and design
objection: AG2 responds that enforcement in practice is weak: regulators are under-resourced, standards get watered down, and companies ship models faster than oversight can keep up, so partial compliance is the default.

target: AG1’s claim that reskilling and job transition programs neutralize economic harm
objection: AG2 argues that even if AI creates new tasks, it still displaces workers and small businesses, weakens bargaining power, and can lower wage growth and increase precarity.

target: AG1’s claim that human-in-the-loop review solves high-stakes AI errors
objection: AG2 says human review does not guarantee correctness when models are biased, humans are pressured by speed or cost, or the system’s objective is misaligned with user welfare; the harms may just change form.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can support critical thinking if used as a tutor
objection: AG2 argues tutoring tools also make it easy to offload thinking through drafts, answers, and translations, which undermines assessment validity and genuine practice, and this is built into product incentives.

target: AG2’s claim that market incentives mean harms will dominate and safeguards cannot work
objection: AG1 objects that incentives cut both ways: liability costs and competition can also push providers to improve reliability and security, especially in visible high-stakes settings.

target: AG2’s claim that responsible AI use is too unreliable to justify AI at all
objection: AG1 argues society already manages imperfect technologies like medicine and transport through regulation, so AI should likewise be judged by its net benefits under controls rather than by the absence of all risk.

target: AG2’s claim that broad refusal is better for marginalized groups
objection: AG1 says refusing AI would forfeit concrete benefits, especially accessibility tools for people with disabilities, and so any claim that AI is bad for society must show these benefits are outweighed, not merely that risks exist.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be judged like medicine with regulation and standards
objection: AG2 argues that AI’s deployment model is much less bounded than medicine: it is broadly deployed, updated iteratively, and embedded into many decisions quickly, making oversight harder and delays more likely.

target: AG1’s claim that audits and continuous governance can reduce bias and safety harms
objection: AG2 says audits often change only what is measured, not what people experience, because teams can optimize fairness metrics while real-world disparities persist through data drift, new cohorts, and shifting goals.

target: AG1’s claim that humans are biased too, so AI bias is not uniquely bad
objection: AG2 replies that AI’s key difference is automation at scale and speed, which amplifies the volume, consistency, and reach of biased outcomes, making the overall effect worse for marginalized groups.

target: AG1’s claim that broad opposition would preserve inequity and block accessibility
objection: AG2 argues that the safer policy is to limit AI broadly because governance cannot reliably prevent recurring privacy, labor, and cognitive harms at scale, especially as systems update and become embedded in decisions.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s concentration problem is just a competition issue fixable by antitrust and interoperability
objection: AG2 says such rules will not undo lock-in easily because dominant providers also control compute, proprietary data pipelines, talent, and distribution via closed APIs, so concentration harms persist.

target: AG1’s claim that training privacy can be solved with curated datasets, minimization, and privacy-preserving training
objection: AG2 objects that strong privacy constraints and consent rules clash with competitive performance and scale, and firms have incentives to cut corners while regulators face a moving target of continuous updates.

target: AG1’s claim that beneficial AI uses can be preserved while restricting unsafe uses
objection: AG2 argues that general-purpose AI systems spill into higher-risk uses through repurposing, surveillance-adjacent applications, and cheating or assessment undermining, so spillover is hard to stop.

target: AG2’s claim that market concentration and training-data privacy make broad AI opposition necessary
objection: AG1 replies that concentration is a competition and regulation problem, not a reason to reject AI, and that privacy can be improved through licensed datasets, data minimization, purpose limits, retention limits, and privacy-preserving training.

target: AG1’s claim that antitrust, interoperability, and data governance can fix structural AI harms
objection: AG2 says these fixes are structurally hard because compute costs, proprietary infrastructure, and changing model pipelines preserve concentration, while privacy and consent constraints are undermined by competitive incentives and continuous updates.

target: AG1’s claim that low-risk applications can be separated from high-risk ones
objection: AG2 argues that general-purpose AI produces spillover: the same systems can be quickly repurposed for automated decisions, surveillance-like uses, or cheating, so use-case separation is unreliable.

target: AG2’s claim that broad opposition is better because safeguards can fail
objection: AG1 says failure of some safeguards is not a reason to reject AI, because society can enforce specific controls tied to risk sources, and broad opposition would push development into less regulated channels.

target: AG1’s claim that oversight can be made privacy-preserving rather than surveillance-heavy
objection: AG2 argues that meaningful monitoring, audits, and training-data enforcement require visibility into systems and sometimes user interactions, which expands the amount of sensitive data at stake and worsens privacy risk.

target: AG1’s claim that harms can be prevented or rolled back after deployment
objection: AG2 says many harms are effectively irreversible once training data is captured or once bias and wrongful decisions have already affected people, so post-rollout control underestimates the damage.

target: AG1’s claim that capability-based or use-case-based regulation can separate good from harmful AI use
objection: AG2 contends that general-purpose models can be repurposed rapidly and boundaries shift with new features, so capability-based rules are hard to enforce and easy to evade.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring and rollback can make AI safe enough
objection: AG2 argues that training-stage privacy and consent harms happen before monitoring, rollback cannot undo many external harms once released, and regulators will always lag behind evolving general-purpose systems.

target: AG2’s claim that dataset provenance, privacy-by-design, and capability rules cannot really govern AI
objection: AG1 answers that dataset provenance and legal licensing can be required, privacy-by-design can reduce memorization and leakage, and capability/integration rules can enforce risk-proportionate allowance rather than blanket rejection.

target: AG1’s claim that dataset provenance and privacy-by-design can reliably solve training-data problems
objection: AG2 says provenance is not practically verifiable end to end, privacy-preserving methods do not eliminate inference or reconstruction risks, and privacy-utility tradeoffs may disproportionately hurt marginalized users.

target: AG1’s claim that pre-deployment prevention and capability rules are sufficient
objection: AG2 argues harms can occur instantly through third-party use before controls catch up, and general-purpose models can be repurposed through prompts, workflows, and tool chaining faster than regulators can police them.

target: AG2’s claim that non-consensual training and irreversible harms justify broad opposition
objection: AG1 responds that imperfect auditability still allows meaningful regulation through sampling audits, certification, disclosure, and documentation, and that prevention and accountability reduce incidence and severity even if they cannot eliminate every harm.

target: AG1’s claim that education harms can be solved by process-based assessments, transparency rules, and AI tutoring designed to build understanding
objection: AG2 says students still have strong incentives to use AI for faster grades and easier work, producing an AI arms race that burdens teachers and weakens genuine learning despite those safeguards.

target: AG1’s claim that AI tutoring can be designed to strengthen reasoning
objection: AG2 objects that even so-called tutoring can supply convincing explanations and answers that students trust without understanding, so the cognitive harm persists if the system is optimized for helpfulness or engagement.

target: AG1’s claim that accountability in education can be achieved without privacy costs
objection: AG2 argues that enforcing transparency and detecting misuse typically requires monitoring student interactions and storing records, which increases privacy risks and creates tradeoffs rather than solving the problem.

target: AG2’s claim that education-side fixes are impossible because of an AI arms race
objection: AG1 replies that schools have adapted to prior technologies before, and that redesigning assessment with oral defenses, process requirements, and scaffolded drafts can mitigate misuse without blanket AI bans.

target: AG2’s claim that AI tutoring inevitably weakens thinking
objection: AG1 contends that AI can be engineered for learning outcomes, such as adaptive practice, misconception targeting, and verification tasks that require students to check and correct solutions.

target: AG2’s claim that accountability inevitably requires surveillance-heavy enforcement
objection: AG1 says privacy risk can be reduced with limited data collection, disclosure-based checks, random reviews, and aggregate audits rather than continuous student monitoring.

target: AG1’s claim that education safeguards are broadly deployable and can be implemented equitably
objection: AG2 argues that process-based assessments, oral defenses, and verification tasks require resources and staff many schools lack, so the safeguards will work better in wealthy settings and widen inequality elsewhere.

target: AG1’s claim that verified understanding can be required to stop outsourcing
objection: AG2 says students can still use AI to generate or validate explanations, creating a circular loop where even the “verification” step is outsourced and genuine human understanding remains unproven.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-minimizing enforcement avoids serious records
objection: AG2 objects that even random checks, logs, and plagiarism-style systems create and accumulate sensitive educational records over time, so retention and surveillance risks remain.

target: AG2’s claim that inequity makes AI education harms unavoidable
objection: AG1 argues AI can reduce inequality if adopted with funding, vetted tools, and minimum guardrails, and that the correct response is supported adoption rather than refusal that preserves existing inequities.

target: AG2’s claim that verification and accountability in education inevitably create privacy burdens
objection: AG1 says verification can be redesigned to require time-bound, locally produced evidence of learning, and enforcement can rely on minimal data, on-device processing, and strict retention limits.

target: AG1’s claim that equity-focused adoption, assessment redesign, and data minimization can make education AI beneficial
objection: AG2 argues these fixes depend on sustained funding and administrative capacity that many institutions lack, so under-resourced schools will implement weaker safeguards and face greater harm.

target: AG1’s claim that process-based or oral assessments can stop AI outsourcing
objection: AG2 says AI can still assist students in real time with planning, drafting, and justifying answers, turning the assessment into an arms race that still fails to measure genuine understanding.

target: AG1’s claim that data-minimized accountability avoids privacy tradeoffs
objection: AG2 contends that any auditing or review still produces sensitive educational records, and institutions often expand retention over time for legal or disciplinary reasons, so the privacy tradeoff persists.

target: AG1’s claim that technical gating, procurement controls, and retention caps can make classroom AI safe
objection: AG2 says assistive and generative uses are not truly separable with general-purpose models, vendors can expand data-hungry capabilities after procurement, and retention limits are undermined by safety or legal incentives, so the safeguards are too fragile to rely on.

target: AG2’s claim that classroom capability gating, procurement change-control, and retention caps cannot work
objection: AG1 responds that schools can enforce hard technical limits on output, write contracts that block telemetry or feature creep, and set deletion-by-default rules with independent audits, so these are policy design problems rather than reasons to oppose AI broadly.

target: AG1’s claim that output gating prevents education harms
objection: AG2 argues that students can still outsource the thinking itself by using AI for hints, planning, and reasoning checks, so restricting full submissions does not solve cognitive overreliance.

target: AG1’s claim that technical controls can keep AI within classroom boundaries
objection: AG2 says these controls are bypassed in practice through prompting, alternate interfaces, peer sharing, and off-platform use, so general-purpose systems are too flexible to contain reliably.

target: AG1’s claim that procurement SLAs and change-control can stop data and feature creep
objection: AG2 objects that vendors can still ship updates altering telemetry, logging, personalization, or integration behavior, and districts or regulators generally lack the capacity to monitor them continuously.

target: AG1’s claim that retention caps solve privacy concerns in education
objection: AG2 argues retention limits merely relocate the privacy tradeoff because schools still need logs for investigations, audits, or disputes, so the underlying privacy cost remains.
